source.title: Residual Stream Analysis with Multi-Layer SAEs
source.authors: Tim Lawson; Lucy Farnik; Conor J. Houghton; Laurence Aitchison

page_placements.theme: Cross-layer feature persistence, drift and redundancy

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to residual-stream activations in language models and reports reconstruction results, providing indirect evidence relevant to V4. It does not test toy-model superposition or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition and discusses sparse features and polysemantic neurons as background, but does not reproduce its toy-model experiment. Its own relevant results concern sparse-autoencoder reconstruction of LLM activations, decoder-vector similarities, and how latents are active across layers. The layer-distribution results do not measure feature overlap across dimensions or feature spread across neurons. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE-method paper. It trains multi-layer SAEs on LLM residual streams and reports how well its own method performs (FVU, delta CE loss, comparisons with single-layer SAEs). It also reports how latents are spread across layers. It takes the sparse-feature or superposition picture as background and never tests whether features are superposed, whether neurons are polysemantic, or whether SAE features are canonical. Reconstruction quality of the authors' own SAE is method performance, not evidence on V4. The layer-spread and decoder-similarity results concern representation drift and duplicate latents, which are different constructs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that MLSAEs match single-layer SAEs on reconstruction and downstream loss. Latents are multi-layer when aggregated over tokens but mostly single-layer per prompt. This multi-layer activity grows with model size, and tuned-lens transformations do not obviously increase it. They argue that representation drift is a significant obstacle to identifying computational variables with SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a single k-sparse autoencoder across residual-stream activations from all layers of language models. It does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method or its tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with underlying model size, expansion factor, sparsity, tuned-lens transformations, and whether activations are aggregated across tokens or examined for one token. The alternative active-layer count also depends strongly on its threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: MLSAE latents are active at multiple layers when aggregated over tokens: variance ratio 54–88%, rising with model size. For a single token, the ratio is only about 1–10%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The layer at which a sparse latent is active varies by token (representation drift across the residual stream).

fits_no_version.finding: Tuned-lens MLSAEs show a lower aggregate variance ratio, 37–41% across expansion factors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aligning layer bases with the tuned lens does not increase multi-layer latent activity.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder-vector pairwise cosine similarities are only slightly heavier-tailed than a random control and lack the positive-control duplicate peak. MMCS is 0.18–0.28.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLSAEs learn few duplicate, layer-specific copies of the same latent.

record.problems: The reconstruction metrics do not establish ground-truth semantic feature recovery. The paper notes that the Gemma 2 2B downstream-loss increase is larger than for other models of similar size. Some layer-distribution findings are conveyed in figures; reported standard deviations for MMCS describe dispersion, not inferential uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for L1 norms, additional threshold-based active-layer counts, entropy summaries, or figure-only per-model layer-distribution values: these characterize cross-layer activation distributions rather than the listed versions' feature overlap, neuron polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry analysis.
No analysis of neuron polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
No analysis of what causes polysemanticity.

Does not test whether LLM features are distributed across neurons. Does not test whether the recovered sparse features are genuine rather than an artefact of the method; it only reports its own SAE's reconstruction.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicity. MMCS is reported only as a proxy for feature splitting within a single SAE.
No test of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels are removed. FVU and delta CE loss are the authors' own method's performance with no superposition baseline, so they cannot show whether sparse features exist. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment testing overlap, near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity arises from competition for limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Tests sparse-autoencoder reconstruction of LLM residual activations, but does not establish ground-truth semantic feature recovery or that features are distributed across many neurons.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model.
Measures similarities between decoder vectors, but does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: It uses sparse dictionary representations to analyze residual-stream information flow without independently testing superposition or the completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.

tranche.reason: The study develops and evaluates MLSAEs and measures their activation distributions across layers; these results do not test a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The two percentages use different denominators: Eq. 11 normalizes by total layer variance; Eq. 12 normalizes by mean within-latent layer variance. The reported ranges describe standard MLSAEs; tuned-lens results differ.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard and tuned-lens MLSAEs on the tested language models
reader_labels.reason: The learned sparse codes reconstruct residual activations with reported FVU values and the paper also evaluates downstream loss after reconstruction; this is indirect evidence for sparse dictionary representations in LLMs (rows r1–r22).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports a higher increase in cross-entropy loss than for other models of similar sizes, limiting how strongly reconstruction results support functional recovery in this condition (rows r11–r12).
